---
title: "Best practices for a step test"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(lactater)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
plex <- requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(suppressMessages(systemfonts::require_font("IBM Plex Sans", fallback = "sans")))
if (plex) options(lactater.font = "IBM Plex Sans")

## one table per section: the topic, what to do, what the studies found, and how strong that evidence is
practice_table <- function(rows) {
  rows |>
    gt() |>
    fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) |>
    cols_label(topic = "", advice = "What to do", evidence = "What the studies found", strength = "Evidence") |>
    cols_width(topic ~ pct(16), advice ~ pct(32), evidence ~ pct(38), strength ~ pct(14)) |>
    tab_style(cell_text(weight = 600), cells_body(columns = topic)) |>
    tab_style(cell_text(v_align = "top"), cells_body()) |>
    tab_style(cell_text(color = "#5b6672"), cells_body(columns = strength)) |>
    gt_lactater()
}
```

A threshold is only as good as the test behind it. From any table of numbers lactater computes 18 thresholds by
default, two more on request (LTP1-Poly-ModD<sub>max</sub>, and Stegmann with recovery samples), and as many fixed or
baseline-plus targets as you set. But it cannot tell whether the athlete came to the test with empty glycogen stores,
or whether the lactate was sampled from the fingertip in one test and the earlobe in the next. This article collects what the literature says
about running a step test and analyzing it, as a checklist.

```{=html}
<div class="test-steps">
  <div class="test-step"><h4>Before</h4><ul>
    <li>Same diet for 24-48 h</li><li>A recovery day before</li><li>Same caffeine, same time of day</li></ul></div>
  <div class="test-step"><h4>Protocol</h4><ul>
    <li>Stages of 3 min or more</li><li>2-3 stages below the first rise</li><li>To exhaustion</li></ul></div>
  <div class="test-step"><h4>Sample</h4><ul>
    <li>Last 30 s of each stage</li><li>Same site and sample type</li><li>A calibrated analyzer</li></ul></div>
  <div class="test-step"><h4>Record</h4><ul>
    <li>Heart rate and RPE every stage</li><li>Room, ergometer, protocol</li><li>Diet and training</li></ul></div>
  <div class="test-step"><h4>Analyze</h4><ul>
    <li>Methods chosen beforehand</li><li>Check the curve</li><li>Report how sure you are</li></ul></div>
</div>
```

Read each point with its evidence in mind. Few come from guidelines: most come from single studies in small groups,
often of trained men, and some from expert reviews. The last column of each table says which: a guideline, a
meta-analysis, a review, single studies (with how many people), or no study we found. A dagger (&dagger;) marks the one
study read from its abstract only.

## What moves the curve

Most of the advice below exists because something other than fitness moves the lactate curve, and with it every
threshold. This sketch shows the direction of each effect in the studies cited below, not its size:

```{r what-moves, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.2, echo = FALSE}
## a schematic: one reference curve, and each effect as a shift of it in the direction the studies found
reference <- function(x) 0.9 + 0.3 * exp(4.2 * (x - 0.3))
effects <- tibble(
  effect = c(
    "Low glycogen", "Caffeine", "Dehydration", "Shorter stages", "Fingertip instead of earlobe",
    "Plasma instead of whole blood"
  ),
  verdict = c(
    "looks fitter", "lower threshold at 2 mmol/L", "looks less fit", "looks fitter", "looks less fit",
    "looks less fit"
  ),
  changed = list(
    function(x) 0.85 * reference(x - 0.04),
    function(x) reference(x) + 0.55 * exp(-((x - 0.45) / 0.25)^2),
    function(x) reference(x + 0.06),
    function(x) reference(x - 0.07),
    function(x) 1.12 * reference(x),
    function(x) reference(x) / 0.7
  ),
  marker = c(4, 2, 4, 4, 4, 4)
) |>
  mutate(effect = factor(effect, levels = effect))
curves <- effects |>
  rowwise() |>
  reframe(
    effect, verdict, marker,
    intensity = seq(0.2, 1, length.out = 120),
    before = reference(intensity),
    after = changed(intensity)
  )
## where a curve last crosses the marker, interpolated between the two points around it
crossing <- function(lactate, intensity, level) {
  i <- max(which(lactate < level))
  intensity[i] + (level - lactate[i]) / (lactate[i + 1] - lactate[i]) * (intensity[i + 1] - intensity[i])
}
crossings <- curves |>
  group_by(effect, verdict, marker) |>
  summarise(
    from = crossing(before, intensity, first(marker)),
    to = crossing(after, intensity, first(marker)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
colours <- lactater:::lactater_colours()
ggplot(curves, aes(intensity)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = marker), colour = colours[["faint"]], linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = before), colour = colours[["faint"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = after), colour = colours[["curve"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = from, xend = to, y = marker, yend = marker), crossings, colour = colours[["accent"]], linewidth = 0.7,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.06, "inch"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.2, y = 7.4, label = verdict), crossings, hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = colours[["muted"]]) +
  facet_wrap(vars(effect), ncol = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%"), breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 8)) +
  labs(
    title = "What moves the lactate curve",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Gray: the usual test; blue: with the change. The green arrow shows how a fixed-concentration threshold moves.",
      "A schematic of the direction of each effect, not its size"
    ),
    x = "Intensity (% of peak)", y = "Lactate (mmol/L)"
  ) +
  theme_lactater() +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(1.2, "lines"))
```

## Before the test: the same athlete every time

The aim is that the only thing that differs between two tests is fitness.

```{r before, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~topic, ~advice, ~evidence, ~strength,
  "Diet and glycogen",
  "Keep the diet of the 24 to 48 h before the test the same for every test, and avoid exercise that empties the
  glycogen stores.",
  "Low glycogen lowers lactate at every intensity and moves the curve to the right, which looks like better
  endurance ([Faude et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200939060-00003)). In 6 trained men, a
  low-carbohydrate diet with training put the 2 and 4 mmol/L thresholds at higher workloads than a high-carbohydrate
  diet after 3 days without training, yet after the high-carbohydrate diet they rode longer at 65% of their maximal
  workload, 49 against 23 min ([Maassen & Busse, 1989](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00637384)).",
  "Review; 1 study, n = 6",
  "Training before the test",
  "Plan at least one day of full recovery before each test, and test at the same time of day in a room at the same
  temperature.",
  "No study tested the rest day itself. In the reliability study of [Pallarés et al.
  (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0163389), 14 trained male cyclists
  had 24 h of full recovery before every test, and were tested between 16:00 and 19:00 at 21-24 &deg;C; the fixed
  and baseline thresholds varied by about 3% between tests.",
  "No study found",
  "Caffeine",
  "Keep caffeine habits the same.",
  "In 8 men, 5 mg/kg of caffeine raised lactate at submaximal intensities and lowered the threshold at 2 mmol/L,
  from an oxygen uptake of 2.71 to 2.13 L/min, while the breakpoint, the 1 mmol/L rise and the 4 mmol/L thresholds did
  not change ([Gaesser & Rich, 1985](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-2008-1025841)).",
  "1 study, n = 8",
  "Hydration",
  "Start every test equally hydrated.",
  "In a meta-analysis of studies that dehydrated adults before exercise, by 3.6% of body mass on average, the oxygen
  uptake at the lactate threshold was 4.4% lower (95% CI 1.7-7.1%; [Deshayes et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-019-01223-5)). In 7 moderately
  trained women, losing 2.6% of body mass moved the Log-log threshold from 72% to 66% of V&#775;O<sub>2max</sub> ([Moquin &
  Mazzeo, 2000](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-200002000-00021)).",
  "Meta-analysis",
  "Time of day",
  "Test at the same time of day, ideally when the athlete usually trains.",
  "In 11 endurance-trained men tested on a rowing ergometer at six times of day, the power at the D<sub>max</sub>
  threshold did not change, but the oxygen uptake and heart rate at it followed a circadian rhythm; the authors advise
  testing at the time the athlete usually trains ([Forsyth & Reilly,
  2004](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-004-1059-8)).",
  "1 study, n = 11",
  "Warm-up and familiarization",
  "Use the same light warm-up every time, and let a new athlete do one familiarization test.",
  "[Pallarés et al. (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0163389) began with a familiarization test, followed
  by 48 h of rest, \"to minimize the bias of
  progressive learning on test reliability\".",
  "No study found"
) |>
  practice_table()
```

## The protocol

```{r protocol, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~topic, ~advice, ~evidence, ~strength,
  "Stage duration",
  "Use stages of at least 3 min, and keep the protocol identical between tests of the same athlete:
  `compare_tests()` notes when it differs.",
  "Shorter stages put the thresholds at higher intensities, and stages of at least 3 min have been recommended
  ([Bentley et al., 2007](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200737070-00002); [Jamnick et al.,
  2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01322-8)). [Jamnick et al.
  (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199794) compared stages of 1 to 10 min in 17 trained
  men.",
  "Reviews",
  "Number of stages",
  "Plan for six or more. lactater needs at least five for Log-log and six for two lactate turn points.",
  "No guideline sets a number. Six or more is common: [Grant et al. (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-002-0608-2)
  used at least six 4-min stages.",
  "No study found",
  "Start and increment",
  "Start low enough for two or three stages below the first rise in lactate.",
  "The methods for LT1 need those stages, and D<sub>max</sub> depends on where the test starts and ends ([Jamnick et
  al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01322-8)).",
  "Review",
  "End of the test",
  "Go to exhaustion when you use methods that rely on the last stage (the D<sub>max</sub> family and LTP2). If the
  athlete stopped during the last stage, enter its time-weighted intensity, or leave it out with `max_intensity`.",
  "These methods change with the final lactate ([Bentley et al.,
  2007](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200737070-00002); [Jamnick et al.,
  2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01322-8)).",
  "Reviews",
  "Treadmill grade",
  "Whatever the grade, keep it the same; 1% mimics running outdoors.",
  "A 1% grade matched the energy cost of outdoor running at 10.5 to 18 km/h in 9 trained male runners ([Jones & Doust,
  1996](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640419608727717)).",
  "1 study, n = 9",
  "Pauses for sampling",
  "Keep pauses short, and the same between tests.",
  "Short pauses to take the sample are common on a treadmill: [Dickhuth et al.
  (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-2007-971105) used 30 s.",
  "No study found"
) |>
  practice_table()
```

## Taking the sample

```{r sample, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~topic, ~advice, ~evidence, ~strength,
  "Timing",
  "Sample in the last 30 s of each stage.",
  "Most studies do ([Goodwin et al., 2007](https://doi.org/10.1177/193229680700100414); [Morton et al.,
  2012](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsm.2010.076380); [Forsyth & Reilly,
  2004](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-004-1059-8)).",
  "Review",
  "Site",
  "Use the same site in every test.",
  "Finger values were higher than earlobe and venous values in 312 trained athletes, and the authors preferred the
  earlobe ([Dassonville et al., 1998](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9638031/)&dagger;). Fingertip and earlobe
  differed by 9.2% on average in cycling, with 95%
  of differences between -25% and +59% ([Moran et al., 2012](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0b013e318225f395)). The
  fingertip read 0.66 mmol/L higher than the earlobe on average, and 0.86 mmol/L between 4 and 8 mmol/L, in double
  poling on a ski ergometer in 40 university students ([Zhong et al.,
  2025](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-024-05585-1)).
  After two 4-min bouts of ergometer rowing, plasma lactate from the fingertip, toe and earlobe did not differ
  significantly in 9 athletes, 4 of them club rowers, although the fingertip read highest ([Forsyth & Farrally,
  2000](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsm.34.1.35)).",
  "4 studies",
  "Skin preparation and hygiene",
  "Wear gloves, clean the site with 70% alcohol and let it dry in the air, wipe away the first drop of blood, do not
  squeeze hard, and put the lancet straight into a sharps container.",
  "As the [World Health Organization (2010)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK138654/) advises. No study we found
  measured how much sweat on the skin changes a
  sample; drying the site is the usual advice.",
  "Guideline",
  "Sample type",
  "Never mix sample types between tests, and report which one you used (`sample` in `lactate_threshold()`).",
  "Plasma lactate was about 50% higher than lactate in red blood cells, and capillary and venous whole blood also
  differed, in 10 healthy men ([Foxdal et al., 1990](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00357603)); whole-blood lactate is
  about 70% of plasma lactate, depending
  on the hematocrit ([Goodwin et al., 2007](https://doi.org/10.1177/193229680700100414)). The fixed concentrations of
  OBLA, Bsln+ and IAT were defined on blood,
  so `lactate_checks()` warns when `sample` says otherwise.",
  "Review",
  "Analyzer",
  "Calibrate it as the manufacturer says, test each athlete on the same device, and do not compare tests run on
  different analyzers.",
  "The typical error of three portable analyzers was 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L depending on the device ([Tanner et al.,
  2010](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-010-1379-9)), and all three read lower than a laboratory analyzer. Six hand-held
  analyzers all read lower than a laboratory
  analyzer, most at the highest
  concentrations, which \"would overestimate the ability of the athlete\" ([Bonaventura et al.,
  2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4306774/)). With four current hand-held analyzers the direction depended on the device: against a
  laboratory analyzer they read 10% lower to 42% higher, and a second laboratory analyzer read 32% lower; at 3 mmol/L
  their 95% prediction intervals were 0.6 to 0.9 mmol/L wide (venous blood; [Mentzoni et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-024-05572-6)).",
  "3 studies"
) |>
  practice_table()
```

## What else to record

```{r record, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~topic, ~advice, ~evidence, ~strength,
  "Heart rate and RPE",
  "Record both at the end of every stage, in the same window as the blood sample. For RPE, read the standard
  instructions before the test, ask how hard the effort feels (not pain), and ask at the same moment of every
  stage.",
  "In a reliability study of 16 male athletes, RPE and heart rate were taken in the last 15 s of each 3-min stage
  ([Lamb et al., 1999](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsm.33.5.336)).",
  "1 study",
  "Expect them to vary",
  "Use heart rate and RPE at a threshold as a rough guide, not a target.",
  "The test-retest limits of agreement of RPE widened as intensity rose, from 0.88 &plusmn; 2.02 units at the first
  stage to -0.13 &plusmn; 2.94 at the fourth, in 16 male athletes ([Lamb et al.,
  1999](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsm.33.5.336)). In 20 men and 16 women, heart rate and RPE at the thresholds
  reproduced poorly between two tests ([Grant et al., 2002](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-002-0608-2)). In 2,560
  adults (median age 28) on treadmills or cycle ergometers, RPE was 10.8 at the last intensity before lactate began to
  rise, 13.6 at 1.5 mmol/L above it (Dickhuth's individual anaerobic threshold) and 14.1 at 4 mmol/L ([Scherr et al.,
  2013](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-012-2421-x)).",
  "3 studies",
  "The conditions",
  "Room temperature and humidity, the ergometer and its settings, the athlete's diet and training in the days
  before.",
  "No study is needed for this one: without it, you cannot tell later why two tests differ.",
  "No study needed"
) |>
  practice_table()
```

The [recording sheet](../step-test-sheet.pdf) has a place for all of this; the [web form](../step-test-form.html) has the
same fields to fill in during the test and downloads a file that `read_recording()` reads; and `recording_sheet()`
copies both, with a CSV template in the columns lactater reads, into your folder. Give lactater the columns with `heart_rate_column`,
`rpe_column` and `rpe_scale` (`"6-20"` or `"CR10"`). Here is a simulated test with heart rate and RPE (the RPE of the simulated tests in `lactate_tests` is simulated too):

```{r}
client <- lactate_tests |>
  filter(test == "untrained") |>
  select(intensity, lactate, heart_rate, rpe)
client

results <- client |>
  lactate_threshold(
    intensity, lactate, heart_rate,
    rpe_column = rpe, rpe_scale = "6-20", sample = "blood", plot = FALSE
  )

results |>
  filter(method %in% c("Log-log", "LTP1", "LTP2", "OBLA 4.0")) |>
  select(method, intensity, heart_rate, rpe)
```

## Analyzing the test

```{r analysis, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~topic, ~advice, ~evidence, ~strength,
  "Choose beforehand",
  "Choose the methods and the curve before you look at the data, and report them. [The methods
  article](methods.html) summarizes the evidence for each method.",
  "Two methods can put the threshold of the same athlete about 30% apart ([Jamnick et al.,
  2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01322-8)), and no curve fit is
  generally accepted ([Faude et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200939060-00003)).",
  "Reviews",
  "Look before you trust",
  "Plot the test, read `lactate_checks()`, and check how well the curve follows the stages and how much each
  threshold rests on one stage with `lactate_diagnostics()` (see [Checking the analysis](checking.html)).",
  "A table of numbers hides a lactate dip, a final plateau or a single bad sample.",
  "No study needed",
  "Report how sure you are",
  "`ci = TRUE` adds confidence intervals.",
  "The precision of a threshold should be known before a change is called real ([Bentley et al.,
  2007](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200737070-00002)).",
  "Review",
  "Know your noise",
  "Measure the typical error on your athletes with your protocol, and give it to `compare_tests()` as `cv`.",
  "The typical error is the standard deviation of the test-retest differences divided by the square root of 2, best
  given as a coefficient of variation ([Hopkins, 2000](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200030010-00001)). It depends
  on the method and the study: D<sub>max</sub> had
  a standard error of measurement of 2.5 W (on a quadratic fit) against 9 to 25 W for other markers in 11 fit adults
  tested at least six times ([Morton et al., 2012](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsm.2010.076380)), but a coefficient of
  variation of
  10.3% against about 3% for the fixed and
  baseline methods in 14 trained cyclists ([Pallarés et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0163389)).",
  "Review",
  "Compare like with like",
  "Keep the protocol, the site, the sample type, the analyzer, the methods and the curve the same between tests of
  the same athlete. See [Comparing tests](compare.html).",
  "Each of them moves the curve on its own (see the sketch above).",
  "No study needed"
) |>
  practice_table()
```

## A checklist for your report

```{r checklist, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~part, ~record,
  "Who", "Sport, sex, age, training status.",
  "Before the test", "Diet, training, caffeine, time of day.",
  "The protocol", "Ergometer, start, increment, stage duration, pauses, how the test ended.",
  "The sample", "Site, timing within the stage, sample type, analyzer.",
  "The analysis", "The methods and how they are defined (for the D<sub>max</sub> family, where the line starts and
  ends), the fitted curve, whether the resting sample was used, the software and its version
  (`packageVersion(\"lactater\")`).",
  "The uncertainty", "Confidence intervals, and the typical error used to judge changes."
) |>
  mutate(done = "&#9744;", .before = 1) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) |>
  cols_label(done = "", part = "", record = "Report") |>
  cols_width(done ~ pct(5), part ~ pct(20), record ~ pct(75)) |>
  tab_style(cell_text(size = px(18)), cells_body(columns = done)) |>
  tab_style(cell_text(weight = 600), cells_body(columns = part)) |>
  gt_lactater()
```
